Soil moisture memory and the timing of first flowering in upland meadows

Ines Albrecht-Vogt1, Samuel Mbeki-Tran2 and Kari Halvorsen1

1 Institute of Mountain Ecosystems, Example University; 2 Department of Soil Science, Sample College

Abstract

Flowering in upland meadows is usually explained by temperature. Using eight years of observations at three sites, we show that the moisture held in the soil after the spring thaw shifts the date of first flowering by up to two weeks, independently of temperature. Wetter springs bring flowering forward, and the effect persists for several weeks after the soil dries.

Keywords: phenology, soil moisture, upland meadows, flowering time

1. Introduction

The timing of flowering decides which pollinators a plant meets and how long its seeds have to ripen before the first frost [1]. In mountain grasslands the growing season is short, and a shift of a few days can change which species set seed in a given year [2].

Most models of flowering time rely on accumulated warmth above a base temperature [3]. Water is usually treated as a constraint that matters only in drought. Yet in upland soils the water left by snowmelt can stay high for weeks, and roots respond to it long after the surface has dried [4].a

2. Methods

2.1 Study sites

We followed three meadows that differ in slope and exposure (Table 1). At each site, observers recorded the first open flower of twelve common species every two days from April to July, and probes logged soil moisture at ten centimetres every hour.

2.2 Model

We modelled the day of first flowering FF as a function of accumulated warmth and of a moisture memory term that decays with a time constant τ (Equation 1):

F=F0−β∫0tθ(s)e−(t−s)/τdsτF = F_0 - \beta \frac{\int_0^t \theta(s) e^{-(t-s)/\tau} ds}{\tau} (1)

The parameters were fitted for each species with a hierarchical model, so that sites with few observations borrow strength from the others [5].

3. Results

Across species, a wetter spring brought first flowering forward by 4.1 days for every 0.1 increase in soil moisture (Figure 1). The effect was strongest on the north slope, where the soil stays wet longest.

Figure 1.

Date of first flowering against mean spring soil moisture, all species and sites. The dashed line is the fitted model.

Open in new tab

The memory term mattered: models without it explained 38% of the variation between years, and models with it explained 61%. The fitted time constant was close to three weeks for most species.

4. Discussion

Our results suggest that upland plants respond not only to the water available on a given day but to a running memory of it. This helps explain why warm, dry springs do not always bring early flowering, and why the order in which species flower changes from year to year [2].

Climate projections for upland regions point to earlier and less reliable snowmelt. If soil moisture memory shortens, flowering may become more tightly tied to temperature, with consequences for the pollinators that rely on a long, staggered season.

a Soil moisture is reported as volumetric water content (m³ of water per m³ of soil).
